Mesh lets nearby phones connect directly to each other, without the internet or a cell signal.\n\nEach phone in the mesh can send, receive, and pass along data for the others.

It depends on the phone. Each phone\'s hotspot accepts a limited number of devices, and the limit is different on every phone.\n\nPhones that can host a hotspot and join another at the same time can pass data along, which lets more phones join the mesh.
Why is it better than Wi-Fi?

Regular Wi-Fi depends on a single router. If you move too far from it, or it stops working, you lose the connection.

• Mesh has no central router. Phones connect to each other directly.
• If one device leaves, the others can stay connected. The exception is the phone hosting the hotspot: if it stops, the phones joined to it are cut off.

Summary: Wi-Fi works best at home or in the office. Mesh is useful where there is no router or internet.
• One phone opens the Home tab and taps Start Hotspot.\n• Other phones join by scanning that phone\'s QR code, or by opening a connect link shared with them.

• If you started the hotspot: tap Stop Hotspot on the Home tab. Every phone joined to your hotspot will be disconnected.\n• If you joined someone else\'s hotspot: tap the X next to the connection on the Home tab.

Each connection is protected by the hotspot's Wi-Fi password, so only people with the password, connect link or QR code can join.

Messages and files are not end-to-end encrypted. Phones that pass your data along could read it.

Other people on the mesh can see your device name and its mesh address. The app does not share your location. It asks for location permission only because older versions of Android require it to find nearby Wi-Fi devices.

Range is normal Wi-Fi range between two phones. Walls and other obstacles shorten it. A phone in between can pass data along, so the mesh can reach farther than one phone alone.

If you host the hotspot on Android 10 or later, you can choose the band:
• 2.4GHz: reaches farther and passes through walls better, but is slower.
• 5GHz: faster, but shorter range.
Staying connected uses a small amount of battery, because your phone keeps Wi-Fi active and may pass data along for others. To save battery, disconnect when you don\'t need Mesh.

Mesh is most useful where the internet or cell service is unavailable or unreliable.

• Disasters: Mesh does not depend on city infrastructure, so rescuers and first responders can keep communicating. If a user is out of range, messages can be passed along through other devices.
• Outages and remote areas: Mesh keeps nearby people connected during power or network outages, or where there is no signal.

• Home: Start a hotspot, or join one with Connect via QR Code Scan or Connect via Entering Connect URI.
• Network: Lists the devices on your mesh, with each device's name, address, ping time and number of hops. Tap a device to ping it.
• Send: This page is dedicated to sending data, whether it be files, photos, videos, or anything in between. You simply select the file, choose the recipient, then send. It creates a list of data sent, so you can keep track of what you've sent, when, and to whom.
• Receive: Shows files sent to you. Accept or decline a transfer, then download it to the folder chosen in Settings, or delete it.
• Chat: One-on-one conversations with other devices on the mesh. The first screen lists your conversations, showing whether each person is online, the latest message and any unread messages. Tap one to open it.
• Log: A technical record of app activity, used for troubleshooting.
• Settings: Change the language, theme, text size, device name and save folder, turn auto finish on or off, and restart the server.
Can I still use Bluetooth for my headphones?
Can I log back into my chat via another phone?
Sadly no. Your chats can be saved, but they are saved onto the device used. Each node is unique.

Project Mesh runs on Android 8.0 or later. Some options, like choosing the Wi-Fi band, need Android 10 or later.\n\nTo pass data along for others, a phone must be able to host a hotspot and join another one at the same time. Not every phone can. If yours can\'t, the app will tell you.
" to learn what a connect URI is"
A connect URI is a link that lets another phone join your hotspot. It starts with meshrabiya:// and holds the details needed to join: network name, password, port and mesh address.
Share it only with people you want on your mesh. Anyone with the link can join, because it contains your hotspot password.
The QR code on the Home tab holds the same link.
URI stands for Uniform Resource Identifier. Meshrabiya is the open-source networking library Project Mesh uses to set up these connections.

What do AUTO, WIFIDIRECT_GROUP and LOCALONLY_HOTSPOT mean?
AUTO (default) lets the app choose. WIFIDIRECT_GROUP hosts with Wi-Fi Direct. LOCALONLY_HOTSPOT hosts with Android's local-only hotspot.

Quick Share says "Can't share 1 file because Wi-Fi Direct is already in use on your phone." What should I do?
Stop the hotspot on this phone or the other phone, then try again. One of them is still using Wi-Fi Direct.

Which band should I use?
5 GHz is faster. 2.4 GHz reaches farther and passes through walls and furniture better, but is slower.

Can I change the hotspot type without losing my connection?
No. You will be disconnected and need to reconnect with the QR code or URI.

What happens if I use Local while connected to a Wi-Fi router?
Phones that can host and join at the same time can stay connected to the router. Other phones leave the router while hosting.
The Log page shows the live log of network events from Meshrabiya and from Project Mesh itself. It is mainly useful for Project Mesh developers. Here is how to read one line:
[15:16:52.290]: the time of the event (hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds).
WifiDirectManager: the part of the networking engine that handled the event.
169.254.33.215: the virtual mesh address of the device that logged it.
Wifi2pChannel initialized: what happened. Here, the Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) channel opened successfully.
